title: Bakken Mineral Rights
metaTitle: Bakken Mineral Rights Buyer | North Dakota & Montana Royalty
metaDescription: Own Bakken oil royalty in the Williston Basin? We buy North Dakota and eastern Montana mineral interests, including tribal allotment and heir situations.
heroLead: The Bakken turned North Dakota ranch families into oil families almost overnight in the 2010s, and a decade on, plenty of those same families are trying to figure out what a steeply declining well is actually still worth.
intro: Nobody who was ranching in McKenzie or Mountrail County before 2008 expected what happened next. The Bakken and the Three Forks formation beneath it turned the Williston Basin into one of the biggest oil plays in the country, and land that had been valued for cattle and wheat suddenly carried mineral rights worth more than the surface. We've talked to owners whose families have run cattle on the same section since statehood, and we've talked to Fort Berthold allottees navigating a mineral estate held partly in trust. Both deserve the same plain explanation of where their interest stands today.

The thing about Bakken wells is they front-load hard. A lot of the money came in the first two or three years of a well's life, and what's left now, on wells drilled a decade or more back, is a much smaller monthly number riding a long, gentle tail. That doesn't mean the interest is worthless. It means the conversation about selling has to start with where a specific well actually sits on its curve, not with what the check looked like in year one.

sections.heading: The Steep Bakken Decline Curve
paragraphs: Bakken and Three Forks horizontal wells typically lose 60 to 70 percent of their initial production within the first year, then keep declining at a slower but still meaningful rate for years after. If your check today is a fraction of what it was in 2013 or 2014, that's not necessarily a red flag on the well; it's the normal shape of an unconventional horizontal. What matters now is how much flatter the decline has become and whether the well still has a meaningful economic life left in it.

This is exactly why timing a sale in the Bakken is different from timing one in a shallower, slower-declining basin. Selling too early, right after a well comes online, means giving up the years where the check is highest. Selling well into the flat tail, where most current Bakken owners already are, is often the more rational moment, because the bulk of the decline has already happened and the remaining upside is limited.

sections.heading: Fort Berthold and Trust Land Considerations
paragraphs: A meaningful share of Bakken production sits under the Fort Berthold Reservation, where mineral interests can be held in trust by the Bureau of Indian Affairs on behalf of individual allottees or the Three Affiliated Tribes. Selling trust or restricted minerals involves a different process than a standard fee mineral sale, often requiring BIA approval and additional paperwork, and not every buyer is set up to handle it correctly or patiently.
If your interest is trust land, tell us that up front. We won't pretend it's a simple transaction, and we'll walk you through what the BIA process actually requires before you commit to anything.

sections.heading: New Wells Still Coming to Old Sections
paragraphs: Because the Bakken and Three Forks are stacked formations with multiple benches, operators have continued to drill infill wells on units that already had production, sometimes years after the first well went in. That means a section that looks fully developed can still see a new well spudded, which resets part of the value equation for anyone holding minerals under it.
Before we make an offer, we check current permitting activity in your township as well as historical production, because a fresh permit nearby changes the picture meaningfully.

faqs.question: Why has your Bakken royalty check dropped so much since it started?
faqs.answer: Steep initial decline is normal for Bakken and Three Forks horizontal wells. Most of the drop happens in the first year or two; a much slower decline follows for years after. A lower check today doesn't mean the well stopped producing.

faqs.question: Are Montana Bakken interests valued differently than North Dakota ones?
faqs.answer: The core, most productive Bakken acreage sits mostly in North Dakota's McKenzie, Mountrail, Williams, and Dunn counties. Eastern Montana Bakken acreage tends to be flank rather than core, generally with lower well density and production, which affects value.

faqs.question: Your mineral interest is held in trust through the BIA. Can you still buy it?
faqs.answer: We can work with trust and restricted Indian mineral interests, but the process runs through BIA approval and takes longer than a standard fee mineral sale. We'll explain the timeline honestly rather than promise a fast close we can't deliver.

faqs.question: Is there still active drilling in the Bakken?
faqs.answer: Yes, though at a slower pace than the 2012-2015 peak. Infill wells still get permitted on developed units, and some operators continue targeting the Three Forks bench beneath the primary Bakken zone.

faqs.question: Should you sell now or wait to see if a new well gets permitted on your section?
faqs.answer: That depends on current activity near you specifically. We check township-level permitting before making an offer, and if there's a live permit nearby that could meaningfully change your value, we'll tell you that directly.
